text:
The Long Way Home: Apollo 13

On the evening of April 11, 1970, a Saturn V rose from Kennedy Space Center carrying three men toward the Moon. Jim Lovell, the commander, was a veteran of three earlier flights and would be the first person to reach the Moon a second time. Fred Haise was making his first spaceflight and was to walk on the lunar surface. The third seat belonged to Jack Swigert, who had joined the crew only days before. The original command module pilot, Ken Mattingly, had been exposed to German measles and was grounded by flight surgeons, so Swigert, the backup, took his place. The launch was nearly flawless. The crew named their command module Odyssey and their lunar lander Aquarius, and for two days the flight went so smoothly that television networks lost interest in broadcasting it.

The trouble had been planted years earlier, long before liftoff. The oxygen tanks aboard the service module each held liquid oxygen at extreme cold, with a heater and a pair of stirring fans inside. Tank 2 had been dropped slightly during a handling accident at the factory. Later, during a pre-launch test, ground crews struggled to empty it and ran its heater from a higher-voltage supply than the thermostat switches were built to handle. The switches welded shut, the heater ran unchecked, and the Teflon insulation on the wiring inside was badly scorched. Nobody knew. The tank passed every check and flew.

About 55 hours into the mission, with the spacecraft roughly 200,000 miles from Earth, Mission Control asked the crew to turn on the fans to stir the oxygen. Swigert flipped the switch. Some minutes later, at about nine o'clock in the evening in Houston, a bang shook the ship. The exposed wires sparked inside tank 2, the oxygen caught fire, and the pressure inside the tank rose until it burst, tearing away an entire panel of the service module and damaging the second tank beside it.

Swigert reported first. "Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here," he said. Lovell followed with the line that became famous: "Houston, we've had a problem." The warning lights told a grim story. Two of the three fuel cells, which made the ship's electricity and water, were dying, and the oxygen supply was draining away. Lovell, looking out of a window, saw gas streaming into space. Within hours it was clear that Odyssey was finished as a ship of any use, and that the Moon landing was off. The only question left was whether the three men could be brought home alive.

The answer lay in the lunar module. Aquarius had been designed to carry two men down to the surface and back up for about two days. Now it had to keep three alive for four. The crew moved into it, shut down Odyssey to save its small reserve of battery power for the final descent, and powered up the lander. Flight director Gene Kranz and his teams worked in shifts around the clock, and engineers across the country joined in, using simulators and slide rules to invent procedures that no one had ever imagined needing.

The first decision was the route. The spacecraft was on a path that would loop it around the Moon and, as designed, back toward Earth, but it was not aimed to hit the planet's narrow reentry corridor. Controllers chose to fly around the Moon first rather than attempt a risky immediate turnaround. About five hours after the explosion, the crew fired the lander's descent engine, a rocket built for landing rather than for steering a stricken mother ship, to speed the return. After swinging behind the Moon, the crew fired it again for a longer burn to shorten the trip. On April 14, they passed about 158 miles above the lunar surface and, because of the position of the Moon in its orbit, reached a distance of nearly 250,000 miles from Earth, farther than any humans before or since.

Then came the hardships of the long coast. Power in Aquarius had to be rationed so tightly that nearly everything was switched off. The cabin temperature fell to near freezing, water condensed on the walls, and the men slept little, if at all. Water was rationed to a few ounces a day, and Haise developed a fever from an infection. Lovell later said he never felt so cold in his life.

The most dramatic problem was the air itself. As three men breathed in a cabin built for two, carbon dioxide began to build up. The lander's filters could not keep pace. The command module carried spare filters, but they were square, and the lander's sockets were round. On the ground, engineers laid out everything the crew had on board: plastic bags, cardboard from a flight manual, spacesuit hoses, and a roll of duct tape. Within hours they had designed a crude adapter and read the steps up to the crew, who built an identical copy in orbit. The carbon dioxide level dropped, and the improvised device held.

As the Earth grew larger, new problems surfaced. The ship had drifted slightly off course, and a manual correction was needed. Without the computer's guidance, Lovell aligned the burn by keeping the Earth's sunlit edge in the window, a method no one had planned. The burn worked. Meanwhile, Ken Mattingly, the man who had been left behind, worked in a simulator with other engineers to write the detailed procedure for restarting the command module from a cold, dead state, a startup sequence that had never been tested, using far less power than anyone had allowed for.

On April 17, the crew prepared for the end. First they discarded the damaged service module, and as it drifted away they saw for the first time that an entire side was missing and scarred. The sight made it clear how close the disaster had been. Then they powered up Odyssey and, last of all, said goodbye to Aquarius, which had saved them, and released it to burn up in the atmosphere.

Reentry came with one last tense wait. As the capsule plunged into the air, the superheated gas around it blocked all radio contact. The blackout was expected to last about four minutes. It stretched on, and on, past the point where the capsule should have been heard. Controllers sat silent, uncertain whether the heat shield had survived. Then, at last, Swigert's voice came through. Parachutes opened, and television viewers around the world watched the capsule drift down into the South Pacific near Samoa. The crew was recovered by the USS Iwo Jima, tired, thin, and bearded, but unhurt. The mission had lasted almost six days.

Apollo 13 is often called a successful failure. It never reached the Moon, yet it showed what a trained team could do when every assumption had been destroyed. The investigation that followed redesigned the oxygen tanks and removed the faulty wiring, and later Apollo flights went on to land on the Moon. The three astronauts and the ground teams were honored, and the mission is remembered less as a defeat than as an extraordinary rescue, carried out at a distance of a quarter of a million miles, by people who refused to give up on the men in that cold little ship.
